title: Before creation
hook: when no form was seen, no sin or virtue, no sun or moon, He alone was (Sukhmani 21)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sunn, the stillness, and your line: when there was nothing. Did you let one silence be full instead of awkward? Today the twenty-first ashtpadi asks a string of questions about that stillness. Day five hundred nineteen.

Children are very good at one kind of question. Where was I before I was born? What was there before the house? Before the town? Before the world? Each answer just moves the question back a step, until a parent says, gently, that's enough for tonight. The first stanza of Sukhmani's twenty-first ashtpadi asks those child's questions on purpose, one after another, and it doesn't send anyone to bed. It walks them all the way back, to before creation.
screen: `WHERE WAS I BEFORE I WAS BORN?` → `BEFORE THE TOWN? BEFORE THE WORLD?` → `ALL THE WAY BACK.`

segments.voice: The stanza is built from questions, each beginning jab, when. In paraphrase: when there was no form to be seen, where would sin or virtue have come from? When He was absorbed in the stillness, against whom could anyone hold a grudge? When there was no color or mark, who could feel joy or sorrow? When there was only the Supreme, by Himself, who could be caught in attachment or doubt? And then the closing line: He set His own play in motion, and Nanak says, there is no other maker. Notice what the questions do. They take the things that fill an ordinary day, being right and wrong, grudges, happiness, grief, worry, and quietly show that, in this picture, none of them is the floor. Before them, under them, there was the One. Yesterday's hymn in raag Maru fills in the sky for the same scene: no day or night, no moon or sun, only the One, in stillness. The word for form here is akaar, shape, outline, something you can see. Before creation there was no akaar at all. Notice, too, what the stanza doesn't say. It doesn't call joys and sorrows fake. In its picture they belong to the play; they just aren't the deepest thing. And there's a strange comfort in that. Whatever you're carrying this week, the grudge or the worry, there was a time before it, and Sukhmani says the One who was there then is here now.
screen: `JAB: A STRING OF WHEN QUESTIONS.` · `NO FORM, NO GRUDGE, NO SORROW.` · `AKAAR: NO SHAPE YET.` · `REAL, BUT NOT THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `HE ALONE WAS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: imagine before the first light. Close your eyes. Picture the room fading: the furniture, then the walls. Then the street, the city, the earth, the sun. Let each go, gently, like lights going out one at a time. Rest there, in the dark and the quiet, before anything. Then, slowly, let things return. Notice what's still here. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru in the stillness. The bell holds the time.
Before creation. Sukhmani asks: with no form yet, no grudge or sorrow, what was there? Its answer: the One alone, setting the play in motion.
Your line: he alone was. Today, when a worry grips you, ask the stanza's question: what was here before this? Then breathe once. Day five hundred nineteen.

howItsDone: Sikhs reciting Sukhmani Sahib's twenty-first ashtpadi hear a series of when-questions about the time before creation, each answered by the One alone.

myth: the stanza says our joys and sorrows are fake
they're real and belong to the play; they're just not the deepest thing.
the stanza is built from a string of questions
each begins jab, when, and walks back to before creation.
the stanza names a helper who made the world with God
its closing line says there is no other maker.

fork.setup: the stanza asks: before any form, when there was only the One, who could hold a grudge? what's the answer it points to?
options: no one: there was only the One.
fork.reveal: no one. with no form and no other, there was nothing to quarrel with. the One alone was, and set the play in motion.

original.note: Gurmukhi: akaar, form or shape; before creation, no akaar could be seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: before creation is a science question about the start of the universe.
what it means: a string of questions that walks back past sin, grudges and sorrow to the One alone.
what a scholar hears: each line pairs jab, when, with tab, then; the sun-and-moon detail comes from Guru Nanak's creation hymn in raag Maru, not from this stanza.

sources.ref: Sukhmani Sahib, ashtpadi 21, pauri 1 (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 290)
Maru Solhe, Guru Nanak (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1035)

notes: Editor review (2026-10-01): the Maru hymn is now named as yesterday's (it was taught on day 518) instead of introduced as new; the narrator no longer states that joys and sorrows are real as fact; the scholar floor no longer claims the jab-tab pattern echoes Maru Solhe and says plainly that sun and moon come from Maru, not Sukhmani.
Paraphrase of ashtpadi 21 pauri 1 (jab akaar ih kachh na drisatetaa ... naanak karanhaar na doojaa): confirm order of questions and wording.
The outline's 'no sun or moon' is supplied here from Maru Solhe (Ang 1035), not from Sukhmani; a Keeper may point to a Sukhmani line instead.
Avoids linking to scientific cosmology on purpose.
